claim: Atherosclerosis preferentially occurs in arterial regions exposed to disturbed blood flow (d-flow).
source: Atherosclerosis preferentially occurs in arterial regions exposed to disturbed blood flow (d-flow), while regions exposed to stable flow (s-flow) are protected.
evidence: This is a well-established statement in the field, supported by citations in the introduction (Chiu and Chien, 2011; Davies, 1995; Kwak et al., 2014; Tarbell et al., 2014).

claim: Regions exposed to stable flow (s-flow) are protected from atherosclerosis.
source: Atherosclerosis preferentially occurs in arterial regions exposed to disturbed blood flow (d-flow), while regions exposed to stable flow (s-flow) are protected.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the abstract and supported by citations (Chiu and Chien, 2011; Davies, 1995; Kwak et al., 2014; Tarbell et al., 2014).

claim: Kallikrein-related peptidase 10 (Klk10) was identified as a flow-sensitive gene in mouse arterial ECs.
source: Previously, we identified kallikrein-related peptidase 10 (Klk10, a secreted serine protease) as a flow-sensitive gene in mouse arterial ECs, but its role in endothelial biology and atherosclerosis was unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: KLK10 is upregulated under s-flow conditions.
source: Here, we show that KLK10 is upregulated under s-flow conditions and downregulated under d-flow conditions using in vivo mouse models and in vitro studies with cultured ECs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, including immunostaining, western blots, qPCR, and ELISA.

claim: KLK10 is downregulated under d-flow conditions.
source: Here, we show that KLK10 is upregulated under s-flow conditions and downregulated under d-flow conditions using in vivo mouse models and in vitro studies with cultured ECs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, including immunostaining, western blots, qPCR, and ELISA.

claim: KLK10 protein expression was significantly higher in ECs in the s-flow RCA compared to the d-flow LCA.
source: Consistent with our previous data (Nam et al., 2009; Ni et al., 2010), KLK10 protein (Figure 1b, c) and mRNA expression (Figure 1d) were significantly higher in ECs in the s-flow RCA compared to the d-flow LCA.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 1b and 1c.

claim: KLK10 mRNA expression was significantly higher in ECs in the s-flow RCA compared to the d-flow LCA.
source: Consistent with our previous data (Nam et al., 2009; Ni et al., 2010), KLK10 protein (Figure 1b, c) and mRNA expression (Figure 1d) were significantly higher in ECs in the s-flow RCA compared to the d-flow LCA.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: KLK10 protein was found in the adventitia and occasionally observed in the subendothelial layer.
source: Interestingly, KLK10 protein was also found in the adventitia and occasionally observed in the subendothelial layer as well (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is observed in immunostaining images shown in Figure 1b.

claim: KLK10 protein expression was reduced in the lesser curvature (LC) compared to the greater curvature region (GC) of the aortic arch.
source: In addition, KLK10 protein expression was reduced in the lesser curvature (LC; the atheroprone aortic arch region that is naturally and chronically exposed to d-flow) compared to the greater curvature region (GC; the atheroprotected aortic arch region that is naturally and chronically exposed to s-flow) as shown by en face immunostaining (Figure 1e, f).
evidence: This is supported by en face immunostaining data shown in Figure 1e and 1f.

claim: KLK10 mRNA was decreased by OS and increased by LS in HAECs.
source: KLK10 mRNA (Figure 1g), KLK10 protein in cell lysates (Figure 1h, j), and secreted protein in the conditioned media (Figure 1j) were decreased by OS and increased by LS, confirming the role of KLK10 as a flow-sensitive gene and protein in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: KLK10 protein in cell lysates was decreased by OS and increased by LS in HAECs.
source: KLK10 mRNA (Figure 1g), KLK10 protein in cell lysates (Figure 1h, j), and secreted protein in the conditioned media (Figure 1j) were decreased by OS and increased by LS, confirming the role of KLK10 as a flow-sensitive gene and protein in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1h and 1i.

claim: Secreted KLK10 protein in the conditioned media was decreased by OS and increased by LS in HAECs.
source: KLK10 mRNA (Figure 1g), KLK10 protein in cell lysates (Figure 1h, j), and secreted protein in the conditioned media (Figure 1j) were decreased by OS and increased by LS, confirming the role of KLK10 as a flow-sensitive gene and protein in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: Klk10 transcript expression is highest in s-flow (E2 and E3) and decreases in response to acute (E5 and E7) and chronic (E6 and E8) d-flow.
source: As shown in the scRNAseq data analysis (Figure 1k; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), Klk10 transcript expression is highest in s-flow (E2 and E3) and decreases in response to acute (E5 and E7) and chronic (E6 and E8) d-flow.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1k.

claim: Klk10 expression is specific to ECs and not expressed in other cell types studied in the carotid artery.
source: It also shows Klk10 expression is specific to ECs and not expressed in other cell types studied in the carotid artery.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1k.

claim: The Klk10 promoter region is open and accessible (indicating active transcription status) only in ECs exposed to s-flow conditions.
source: Similarly, scATACseq data (Figure 1i; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showed that the Klk10 promoter region is open and accessible (indicating active transcription status) only in ECs exposed to s-flow conditions but closed and inaccessible (indicating inactive transcription status) in ECs under d-flow conditions and all other non-EC types.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell ATAC sequencing data shown in Figure 1l.

claim: The Klk10 promoter region is closed and inaccessible (indicating inactive transcription status) in ECs under d-flow conditions and all other non-EC types.
source: Similarly, scATACseq data (Figure 1i; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showed that the Klk10 promoter region is open and accessible (indicating active transcription status) only in ECs exposed to s-flow conditions but closed and inaccessible (indicating inactive transcription status) in ECs under d-flow conditions and all other non-EC types.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell ATAC sequencing data shown in Figure 1l.

claim: Transfection of HAECs with plasmids to overexpress KLK10 reduced THP-1 monocyte adhesion to the ECs in response to TNFα and under basal conditions.
source: In addition, transfection of HAECs with plasmids to overexpress KLK10 reduced THP-1 monocyte adhesion to the ECs in response to tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) and under basal conditions (Figure 2a; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by monocyte adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Treatment with rKLK10 significantly inhibited monocyte adhesion to HAECs in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Next, we pretreated HAECs overnight with increasing concentrations of rKLK10, followed by TNFα treatment (5 ng/ml for 4 hr). Treatment with rKLK10 significantly inhibited monocyte adhesion to ECs in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by monocyte adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The anti-inflammatory effect of rKLK10 was lost if rKLK10 was heated.
source: Of note, the anti-inflammatory effect of rKLK10 was lost if rKLK10 was heated, implicating the importance of the enzymatic activity or native conformation of KLK10 (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by monocyte adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Treatment with rKLK10 significantly inhibited mRNA and protein expression of VCAM1 and ICAM1.
source: Furthermore, treatment with rKLK10 significantly inhibited mRNA and protein expression of the proinflammatory adhesion molecules vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM1) and intracellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1) (Figure 2c–g).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 2c-g.

claim: rKLK10 treatment inhibited OS-induced monocyte adhesion in HAECs.
source: rKLK10 treatment inhibited OS-induced monocyte adhesion in HAECs (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is supported by monocyte adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of KLK10 significantly increased monocyte adhesion under LS conditions.
source: In contrast, siRNA-mediated knockdown of KLK10 significantly increased monocyte adhesion under LS conditions (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by monocyte adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Treatment with rKLK10 in vivo dramatically reduced VCAM1 expression in the d-flow (LC) region in the aortic arch of mice.
source: Treatment with rKLK10 in vivo (intravenous injection every 2 days for 5 days at 0.6 mg/kg) dramatically reduced VCAM1 expression in the d-flow (LC) region in the aortic arch of these mice (Figure 2j, k).
evidence: This is supported by en face immunostaining data shown in Figure 2j and 2k.

claim: KLK10 prevented phosphorylation (p-Ser536) and trans-nuclear location of p65 in response to TNFα.
source: We first found that KLK10 prevented phosphorylation (p-Ser536) and trans-nuclear location of p65, two important markers of NFκB activation, in response to TNFα (Figure 3a–d).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a-d.

claim: KLK10 prevented trans-nuclear location of p65 in response to acute shear challenge using LS condition.
source: KLK10 also prevented trans-nuclear location of p65 in response to acute shear challenge using LS condition (Figure 3e, f), which is well known to induce robust and transient NFκB activation (Baeriswyl et al., 2019; Baeyens et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2003; Coleman et al., 2020; Lay et al., 2019; Mohan et al., 1997; Petzold et al., 2009; Stefanini et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3e and 3f, and by citations to previous work.

claim: Overnight rKLK10 pretreatment prevented the permeability increase induced by thrombin in HAECs.
source: As a positive control, thrombin treatment increased the permeability of HAECs as measured by increased binding of fluorescently labeled (FITC)-avidin to biotin-gelatin as reported previously (Dubrovskyi et al., 2013). Overnight rKLK10 pretreatment prevented the permeability increase induced by thrombin in HAECs (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: This is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: rKLK10 reduced the permeability induced by OS.
source: Similarly, rKLK10 reduced the permeability induced by OS (Figure 4c, d).
evidence: This is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 4c and 4d.

claim: Injection with rKLK10 significantly reduced atherosclerosis development and macrophage accumulation in the LCA of Apoe−/− mice.
source: Injection with rKLK10 by tail vein (twice per week at 0.6 mg/kg for 3 weeks post-PCL surgery) significantly reduced atherosclerosis development and macrophage accumulation in the LCA (Figure 5a–e).
evidence: This is supported by histological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 5a-e.

claim: rKLK10 treatment showed no effect on plasma levels of total, LDL, and HDL cholesterols and triglycerides.
source: The rKLK10 treatment showed no effect on plasma levels of total, LDL (low-density lipoprotein), and HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterols and triglycerides (Figure 5f–i).
evidence: This is supported by plasma lipid analysis data shown in Figure 5f-i.

claim: Atherosclerotic plaque formation in the LCA was significantly reduced in the KLK10 overexpressing mice compared to the luciferase control.
source: Atherosclerotic plaque formation in the LCA was significantly reduced in the KLK10 overexpressing mice compared to the luciferase control (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by gross plaque images and quantification shown in Figure 6b and 6c.

claim: Plaque area in the LCA was decreased in KLK10 overexpressing mice compared to luciferase control.
source: Further assessment of the carotid artery sections by histochemical staining with hematoxylin and eosin (Figure 6d, e) showed decreased plaque area in the LCA of these mice.
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining and quantification shown in Figure 6d and 6e.

claim: Higher levels of KLK10 staining were found at the endothelial layer in the LCA and RCA of KLK10 overexpressing mice.
source: However, we found higher levels of KLK10 staining at the endothelial layer in the LCA and RCA (Figure 6f, g), as well as in the lung tissue samples as shown by western blot (Figure 6h, i).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6f and 6g.

claim: Higher levels of KLK10 were found in the lung tissue samples of KLK10 overexpressing mice.
source: However, we found higher levels of KLK10 staining at the endothelial layer in the LCA and RCA (Figure 6f, g), as well as in the lung tissue samples as shown by western blot (Figure 6h, i).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6h and 6i.

claim: No significant difference was observed in plasma total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDLc, LDLc, and non-HDLc in the KLK10-injected mice compared to the control mice.
source: We observed no significant difference in plasma total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDLc, LDLc, and non-HDLc (Figure 6j–n) in the KLK10-injected mice compared to the control mice.
evidence: This is supported by plasma lipid analysis data shown in Figure 6j-n.

claim: KLK10 expression was significantly reduced at the endothelial layer in arteries with significant plaques (grades 4–6) than less-diseased arteries (grades 1–3).
source: KLK10 and CD31 immunostaining demonstrated that KLK10 expression was significantly reduced at the endothelial layer in arteries with significant plaques (grades 4–6; Figure 7a, b) than less-diseased arteries (grades 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data from human coronary artery sections shown in Figure 7a, 7b, and 7c.

claim: KLK10 is a member of the kallikrein-related peptidase 'KLK' family of 15 secreted serine proteases.
source: KLK10 was initially identified as a normal epithelial cell-specific 1 (NES1) (Diamandis et al., 2000) and is a member of the kallikrein-related peptidase 'KLK' family of 15 secreted serine proteases, which are found as a gene cluster on human chromosome (19q13.4) (Yousef et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Diamandis et al., 2000; Yousef et al., 1999).

claim: The tissue KLKs are distinct from plasma kallikrein, which is encoded on a separate chromosome (4q35).
source: The tissue KLKs are distinct from plasma kallikrein, which is encoded on a separate chromosome (4q35) (Yousef and Diamandis, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Yousef and Diamandis, 2003).

claim: KLK10 was initially discovered as a potential tumor suppressor with its expression downregulated in breast, prostate, testicular, and lung cancer.
source: KLK10 was initially discovered as a potential tumor suppressor with its expression downregulated in breast, prostate, testicular, and lung cancer (Goyal et al., 1998; Liu et al., 1996; Hu et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Goyal et al., 1998; Liu et al., 1996; Hu et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2010).

claim: KLK10 is overexpressed in ovarian, pancreatic, and uterine cancer.
source: Further studies, however, showed a more complex story as KLK10 is overexpressed in ovarian, pancreatic, and uterine cancer (Luo et al., 2003; Yousef et al., 2005; Dorn et al., 2013; Tailor et al., 2018; Sotiropoulou et al., 2009; Bharaj et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Luo et al., 2003; Yousef et al., 2005; Dorn et al., 2013; Tailor et al., 2018; Sotiropoulou et al., 2009; Bharaj et al., 2002).

claim: Treatment of mice in vivo with rKLK10 decreased arterial endothelial inflammation in d-flow regions.
source: Furthermore, treatment of mice in vivo with rKLK10 decreased arterial endothelial inflammation in d-flow regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 2j and 2k.

claim: rKLK10 injection inhibited atherosclerosis in Apoe−/− mice.
source: Additionally, rKLK10 injection or ultrasound-mediated transfection of Klk10-expressing plasmids inhibited atherosclerosis in Apoe−/− mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ultrasound-mediated transfection of Klk10-expressing plasmids inhibited atherosclerosis in Apoe−/− mice.
source: Additionally, rKLK10 injection or ultrasound-mediated transfection of Klk10-expressing plasmids inhibited atherosclerosis in Apoe−/− mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: KLK10 protected against d-flow-induced permeability dysfunction in human artery ECs.
source: Functionally, KLK10 protected against d-flow-induced permeability dysfunction and inflammation in human artery ECs, as determined by NFκB activation, expression of vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 and intracellular adhesion molecule 1, and monocyte adhesion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: KLK10 protected against d-flow-induced inflammation in human artery ECs.
source: Functionally, KLK10 protected against d-flow-induced permeability dysfunction and inflammation in human artery ECs, as determined by NFκB activation, expression of vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 and intracellular adhesion molecule 1, and monocyte adhesion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: KLK10 is a flow-sensitive endothelial protein that serves as an anti-inflammatory, barrier-protective, and anti-atherogenic factor.
source: KLK10 is a flow-sensitive endothelial protein that serves as an anti-inflammatory, barrier-protective, and anti-atherogenic factor.
evidence: This is the concluding statement of the abstract, summarizing the findings of the study.

claim: Treatment with rKLK10 significantly inhibited migration and tube formation in HUVECs.
source: Treatment of human umbilical vein ECs (HUVECs) with rKLK10 significantly inhibited migration and tube formation, but not proliferation and apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by scratch assay and tube formation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with rKLK10 did not affect proliferation and apoptosis in HUVECs.
source: Treatment of human umbilical vein ECs (HUVECs) with rKLK10 significantly inhibited migration and tube formation, but not proliferation and apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 and TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Injection of rKLK10 at 0.6 mg/kg dose increased its plasma level to a peak of ~1600 ng/ml with a t1/2 of 4.5 hr.
source: Injection of rKLK10 at 0.6 mg/kg dose increased its plasma level to a peak of ~1600 ng/ml with a t1/2 of 4.5 hr, becoming undetectable by 24 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: rKLK10 became undetectable in plasma by 24 hr after injection.
source: Injection of rKLK10 at 0.6 mg/kg dose increased its plasma level to a peak of ~1600 ng/ml with a t1/2 of 4.5 hr, becoming undetectable by 24 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: KLK10 protein signals observed in the subendothelial and adventitial layers are likely to be originated from ECs.
source: This suggests that KLK10 protein observed in nonendothelial layers, including the adventitia and subendothelial layer (Figure 1b), is unlikely to be originated from cell types other than ECs.
evidence: This is inferred from the scRNAseq and scATACseq data showing that Klk10 is primarily expressed by ECs, and the fact that KLK10 is a secreted protein.

claim: The anti-inflammatory effect of KLK10 is unique in comparison to other KLKs expressed in ECs, including KLK8 and KLK11.
source: Interestingly, the anti-inflammatory effect of KLK10 seems to be unique in comparison to other KLKs expressed in ECs, including KLK8 and KLK11.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2, where rKLK10, but not rKLK8 or rKLK11, inhibited endothelial inflammation.

claim: rKLK10, but not rKLK8 or rKLK11, inhibited endothelial inflammation in response to TNFα in HAECs.
source: We found that rKLK10, but not rKLK8 or rKLK11, inhibited endothelial inflammation in response to TNFα in HAECs (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by monocyte adhesion assay and western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: D-flow induces endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis in large part by regulating flow-sensitive coding and noncoding genes, as well as epigenetic modifiers.
source: D-flow induces endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis in large part by regulating flow-sensitive coding and noncoding genes, as well as epigenetic modifiers (Davies, 1995; Kumar et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2019; Dunn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Davies, 1995; Kumar et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2019; Dunn et al., 2014).

claim: Klk10 was identified as one of the most flow sensitive genes, with high expression under s-flow and low expression under d-flow conditions.
source: Among the flow-sensitive genes, kallikrein-related peptidase 10 (Klk10) was identified as one of the most flow sensitive; with high expression under s-flow and low expression under d-flow conditions (Ni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Ni et al., 2010).

claim: The KLKs are produced as inactive full-length prepropeptides, which are then secreted and activated by a complex process to yield active extracellular enzyme.
source: Typically, the KLKs are produced as inactive full-length prepropeptides, which are then secreted and activated by a complex process to yield active extracellular enzyme (Yousef and Diamandis, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Yousef and Diamandis, 2003).

claim: KLKs are involved in a wide variety of processes ranging from skin desquamation to tooth development, hypertension, and cancer.
source: KLKs are involved in a wide variety of processes ranging from skin desquamation to tooth development, hypertension, and cancer (Madeddu et al., 2007; Clements et al., 2004; Yousef and Diamandis, 2001; Pampalakis and Sotiropoulou, 2007; Margolius, 1998; Campbell, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Madeddu et al., 2007; Clements et al., 2004; Yousef and Diamandis, 2001; Pampalakis and Sotiropoulou, 2007; Margolius, 1998; Campbell, 2001).

claim: Endothelial cells are equipped with several mechanosensors located at the luminal and abluminal surface, cell–cell junction, and cytoskeleton, which detect fluid shear stress and trigger cascades of signaling pathways and cellular responses.
source: Endothelial cells (ECs) are equipped with several mechanosensors located at the luminal and abluminal surface, cell–cell junction, and cytoskeleton, which detect fluid shear stress and trigger cascades of signaling pathways and cellular responses (Kwak et al., 2014; Tarbell et al., 2014; Mack et al., 2017; Tzima et al., 2005; Li et al., 2015; Chachisvilis et al., 2006; Florian et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Kwak et al., 2014; Tarbell et al., 2014; Mack et al., 2017; Tzima et al., 2005; Li et al., 2015; Chachisvilis et al., 2006; Florian et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2016).

claim: NFκB is a well-known proinflammatory transcription factor, which induces expression of VCAM1 and ICAM1 and subsequent monocyte adhesion to ECs.
source: Since NFκB is a well-known proinflammatory transcription factor, which induces expression of VCAM1 and ICAM1 and subsequent monocyte adhesion to ECs (Baeriswyl et al., 2019; Baeyens et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2003; Coleman et al., 2020; Lay et al., 2019; Mohan et al., 1997; Petzold et al., 2009; Stefanini et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2013), we tested whether KLK10 inhibits NFκB activation in response to shear stress and TNFα.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations (Baeriswyl et al., 2019; Baeyens et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2003; Coleman et al., 2020; Lay et al., 2019; Mohan et al., 1997; Petzold et al., 2009; Stefanini et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2013).

claim: Acute shear challenge using LS condition is well known to induce robust and transient NFκB activation.
source: KLK10 also prevented trans-nuclear location of p65 in response to acute shear challenge using LS condition (Figure 3e, f), which is well known to induce robust and transient NFκB activation (Baeriswyl et al., 2019; Baeyens et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2003; Coleman et al., 2020; Lay et al., 2019; Mohan et al., 1997; Petzold et al., 2009; Stefanini et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations (Baeriswyl et al., 2019; Baeyens et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2003; Coleman et al., 2020; Lay et al., 2019; Mohan et al., 1997; Petzold et al., 2009; Stefanini et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2013).

claim: Normal plasma KLK10 levels in humans are ~0.5 ng/ml, with a range from nearly undetectable to ~20 ng/ml in various cancers patients.
source: In humans, normal plasma KLK10 levels are ~0.5 ng/ml, with a range from nearly undetectable to ~20 ng/ml in various cancers patients (Luo et al., 2003; Planque et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations (Luo et al., 2003; Planque et al., 2008).

claim: Plasma KLK10 level in Apoe−/− mice is in the range of 5–10 ng/ml.
source: Our mouse KLK10 ELISA study (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showed that plasma KLK10 level in Apoe−/− mice is in the range of 5–10 ng/ml.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: KLK10 levels in HAECs exposed to the anti-inflammatory LS was ~0.3 ng/ml.
source: We found that KLK10 levels in HAECs exposed to the anti-inflammatory LS was ~0.3 ng/ml, which decreased to ~0.13 ng/ml by the proinflammatory OS (Figure 1j).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: KLK10 levels in HAECs decreased to ~0.13 ng/ml by the proinflammatory OS.
source: We found that KLK10 levels in HAECs exposed to the anti-inflammatory LS was ~0.3 ng/ml, which decreased to ~0.13 ng/ml by the proinflammatory OS (Figure 1j).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: 1–10 ng/ml of rKLK10 inhibits permeability and inflammation in HAECs.
source: In functional studies, we found that 1–10 ng/ml of rKLK10 inhibits permeability and inflammation in HAECs, which falls within the reasonable physiological range.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The effect of rKLK10 on monocyte adhesion is weaker than that of KLK10 overexpression using the plasmid vector.
source: It is also worth noting that the effect of rKLK10 on monocyte adhesion (Figure 2b) is weaker than that of KLK10 overexpression using the plasmid vector (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: KLK10 produced from plasmid directly in HAECs is processed to be more effective than the rKLK10 produced and processed in CHO cells.
source: We speculate that KLK10 produced from plasmid directly in HAECs is processed to be more effective than the rKLK10 produced and processed in CHO cells, which underwent multiple purification steps and storage conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion based on the observation that plasmid-driven KLK10 expression is more effective than rKLK10 treatment.

claim: Klk8 and Klk11 are two other KLK members expressed in ECs.
source: Analysis of the sc-RNAseq dataset showed that Klk8 and Klk11 are two other KLK members expressed in ECs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: All non-EC types in the carotid artery express nearly undetectable levels of Klk10 mRNA transcript.
source: Importantly, all non-EC types in the carotid artery express nearly undetectable levels of Klk10 mRNA transcript and also display closed chromatin accessibility in the Klk10 promoter region, demonstrating that Klk10 is primarily expressed by ECs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by scRNAseq and scATACseq data shown in Figure 1k and 1l.

claim: All non-EC types in the carotid artery display closed chromatin accessibility in the Klk10 promoter region.
source: Importantly, all non-EC types in the carotid artery express nearly undetectable levels of Klk10 mRNA transcript and also display closed chromatin accessibility in the Klk10 promoter region, demonstrating that Klk10 is primarily expressed by ECs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by scATACseq data shown in Figure 1l.

claim: Klk10 is primarily expressed by ECs.
source: Importantly, all non-EC types in the carotid artery express nearly undetectable levels of Klk10 mRNA transcript and also display closed chromatin accessibility in the Klk10 promoter region, demonstrating that Klk10 is primarily expressed by ECs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by scRNAseq and scATACseq data shown in Figure 1k and 1l.

claim: KLK10 may serve as potential anti-atherogenic therapeutic targets.
source: KLK10 may serve as potential anti-atherogenic therapeutic targets.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The protective effects of rKLK10 or plasmid-driven KLK10 expression on endothelial inflammation, barrier function, and atherosclerosis suggest its therapeutic potential for atherosclerosis treatment.
source: The protective effects of rKLK10 or plasmid-driven KLK10 expression on endothelial inflammation, barrier function, and atherosclerosis suggest its therapeutic potential for atherosclerosis treatment.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) and scATAC sequencing (scATACseq) study using the partial carotid ligation mouse model showed flow-regulated Klk10 expression at the epigenomic and transcription levels.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) and scATAC sequencing (scATACseq) study using the partial carotid ligation mouse model showed flow-regulated Klk10 expression at the epigenomic and transcription levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 1k and 1l.

claim: The proatherogenic and atheroprotective effects of d-flow and s-flow are mediated in part by the global changes in endothelial cell (EC) gene expression.
source: The proatherogenic and atheroprotective effects of d-flow and s-flow are mediated in part by the global changes in endothelial cell (EC) gene expression, which regulates endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and atherosclerosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is a well-established concept in the field.

claim: Global changes in endothelial cell gene expression regulate endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and atherosclerosis.
source: The proatherogenic and atheroprotective effects of d-flow and s-flow are mediated in part by the global changes in endothelial cell (EC) gene expression, which regulates endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and atherosclerosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is a well-established concept in the field.
